planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or set out onion sets as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; as a long-day type Bedfordshire Champion needs the longer summer daylight of temperate northern latitudes to bulb well.

directions: Bedfordshire Champion is a Victorian-era English heirloom maincrop onion, introduced in the 1860s-70s and still valued for its large, well-shaped, straw-yellow globes and reliable heavy cropping. Sow indoors in late winter or set out sets after the ground has warmed, spacing plants to let bulbs size up fully, and keep weeds down since onions compete poorly with neighboring growth. It is prized among long-day storage onions for holding firm for many months when cured properly, making it a staple for root-cellar keeping. Lift once the foliage has fallen over and dried, then cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded location before trimming and storing.

planting.note: Plant onion sets as soon as the soil is workable in early spring, pushing each bulb in root-side down until just the tip shows; Sturon is a Dutch-bred long-day maincrop onion widely sold as sets for spring planting in temperate climates.

directions: Sturon is one of the most widely planted Dutch maincrop onion cultivars, grown from sets for its round, golden-brown-skinned bulbs and dependably heavy yields. Plant sets shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil and firm the soil around them so birds cannot pull the sets loose, then keep the row weed-free while bulbs size up over summer. It is valued as a strong keeper, with well-cured bulbs commonly holding firm in storage for several months past harvest. Bend or wait for tops to fall over naturally before lifting, then dry the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot before trimming and storing.

planting.note: Sow seed indoors in mid-winter, 12-14 weeks before the last frost, to give this giant exhibition type the long growing season it needs; transplant out once hardened off and frost danger has passed.

directions: Kelsae is a British giant exhibition onion bred to produce enormous, mild-flavored globes that regularly place among the largest onions grown at horticultural shows. Start seed early under lights, prick out into individual pots, and transplant into deeply dug, heavily enriched soil with generous spacing so each bulb has room to reach show-winning size. Feed and water generously through the growing season, since exhibition size depends on sustained, uninterrupted growth rather than stress-hardening. Because the huge, thin-skinned bulbs are milder and less pungent than standard storage onions, they are best used soon after harvest rather than held for long-term storage.

planting.note: Plant sets or transplants in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Santé is a Dutch-bred long-day storage onion selected for uniform, semi-globe bulbs and strong disease resistance in the field.

directions: Santé is a widely grown European storage onion producing firm, semi-globe bulbs with tight straw-yellow skin and pungent, long-keeping flesh. Plant sets or young transplants in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow full bulb development, and keep the row weeded since onions are shallow-rooted and slow to establish. It has good field tolerance to downy mildew and onion white rot compared with many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice in humid climates. Harvest once most tops have fallen over, cure thoroughly in a warm, airy location, and expect several months of firm storage from well-cured bulbs.

planting.note: In mild-winter regions start seed indoors in late summer and transplant in fall for a spring harvest; in cold-winter climates sow in early spring instead. Long Red Florence is an Italian heirloom that can also be pulled young as a sweet salad onion before bulbing fully.

directions: Long Red Florence is a traditional Tuscan heirloom onion grown for its elongated, torpedo-shaped bulbs of glossy deep-red skin and mild, sweet white-and-red flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and space plants closely enough to encourage the characteristic slender shape rather than a rounded bulb. It can be harvested at three distinct stages: pulled very young as a scallion-like salad onion, at mid-size for grilling whole, or left to mature into a full torpedo bulb for slicing raw over pizza and salads. Because its flesh is milder and higher in moisture than standard storage onions, plan to use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it in long-term storage.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil is workable; Southport Yellow Globe is a long-day heirloom best suited to northern gardens with a full summer growing season.

directions: Southport Yellow Globe is a nineteenth-century American heirloom onion from Southport, Connecticut, and the yellow-skinned counterpart to the better-known Southport White Globe and Southport Red Globe. It forms well-rounded, medium-large globes of tan-gold skin over firm, pungent, long-storing flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and keep the bed weeded, since this open-pollinated heirloom is slower to establish than modern hybrids. Harvest once most of the tops have fallen and dried, cure fully in a warm, airy spot, and expect good keeping quality typical of the classic Southport globe strains.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden as soon as the soil can be worked; Yellow Globe Danvers is a long-day heirloom bred for the summer day length of northern latitudes.

directions: Yellow Globe Danvers is a classic American heirloom onion developed near Danvers, Massachusetts, in the 1850s and grown for generations as a reliable, well-storing globe onion. The medium-sized bulbs form tight round globes with papery yellow-brown skin over firm, pungent flesh well suited to cooking rather than fresh eating. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin or space plants so bulbs can round out fully without crowding. Lift once the tops have fallen over and dried, cure in a warm, airy location for a couple of weeks, and expect this variety to store as well as any classic long-day storage onion.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil can be worked; as a long-day type Long Keeper performs best in northern and mid-latitude gardens with a full summer to size up.

directions: Long Keeper lives up to its name as a pungent yellow storage onion selected specifically for exceptional shelf life, commonly holding firm for eight months to a year in a cool, dry pantry. Transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil and give plants full sun and consistent moisture through bulb formation, then reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall. Because the flavor is sharp and the flesh dense, it is best suited to cooked dishes rather than fresh raw use. Cure the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot for several weeks before storage, since a complete cure is what gives this variety its outstanding keeping quality.

planting.note: Plant sets in early autumn, about a month before the first hard frost, so plants establish roots before winter; Hyskin is a traditional British autumn-planting onion selected for reliable overwintering.

directions: Hyskin is a hardy British heirloom onion grown from autumn-planted sets to give an earlier harvest the following summer than spring-planted types. Push the small bulbs into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving just the tip exposed, and mulch lightly in the coldest regions to protect against hard freezes. Growth resumes as days lengthen in spring, and the brown-skinned bulbs size up quickly ahead of standard maincrop onions. Because overwintered onions generally store less well than spring-planted maincrop types, plan to use Hyskin bulbs within a few months of the early-summer harvest.

planting.note: Plant sets in early autumn so roots establish before winter dormancy; Radar is a modern F1 overwintering onion bred for uniform round bulbs and reliable cold survival through a mild winter.

directions: Radar is a widely grown F1 overwintering onion bred to give gardeners a bulb harvest weeks ahead of spring-sown types by getting a head start on root growth before the ground freezes. Set out young bulbs in firmed, well-drained soil in early autumn, leaving the tip just above the surface, and keep beds weed-free through the mild winter growth period. The straw-yellow, semi-globe bulbs bulk up rapidly once spring days lengthen, typically ready weeks earlier than spring-set maincrop onions. Because overwintered bulbs are generally milder and less firm than maincrop storage onions, use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it long term.

planting.note: Plant sets in early autumn so plants establish before winter; Electric is a red-skinned overwintering onion bred for cold survival, giving an earlier red-onion harvest than spring planting allows.

directions: Electric is a popular overwintering red onion prized for combining the deep reddish-purple skin of a standard red onion with the earlier harvest timing of autumn-planted sets. Push sets into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving the tip exposed, and provide light winter protection only in the coldest parts of its range. Growth resumes quickly as spring days lengthen, and bulbs color up well even under the shorter, cooler growing period overwintering onions experience. Because overwintered red onions tend to be milder and slightly less firm than maincrop reds, plan to use the harvest within a few months of the early-summer lift.

planting.note: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Prisma is a Dutch-bred shallot valued for uniform, high-yielding clusters.

directions: Prisma is a modern Dutch shallot cultivar bred for uniform, copper-skinned, round-to-oval bulbs and dependably heavy yields, making it one of the more widely available shallots in the commercial seed trade. Plant sets shallowly in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a tight cluster of several bulbs by midsummer. Keep the bed evenly moist during active growth and taper off watering once the foliage begins to yellow and topple over. Cure the harvested cluster in a warm, airy, shaded spot for a couple of weeks before separating and storing, where well-cured Prisma bulbs keep respectably for a shallot, typically several months.

planting.note: Plant bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in early spring as soon as the soil is workable; Camelot is a British-trade shallot selected for round, coppery-brown bulbs and heavy cropping.

directions: Camelot is a round-bulbed shallot cultivar grown for its coppery-brown skin, dense clove-free flesh, and consistently heavy yields from each planted set. Set bulbs shallowly in loose, fertile, well-drained soil and keep the row weeded, since shallots have a shallow, easily shaded root system. Each bulb divides into a cluster of several new bulbs over the growing season, ready to lift once the foliage yellows and falls over in midsummer. Cure the whole cluster in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks before separating the bulbs for storage or replanting a portion for next year's crop.

planting.note: Separate cloves and plant pointed end up, about 2 inches deep, in fall around the time of first frost; Rose de Lautrec holds Protected Geographical Indication status in France for garlic grown around the town of Lautrec in the Tarn region.

directions: Rose de Lautrec is a celebrated French softneck garlic named for the town of Lautrec, where it has earned Protected Geographical Indication status for its rose-pink-blushed skin and distinctive, refined flavor. Plant cloves pointed end up in loose, well-drained soil in fall, mulching lightly in colder regions to buffer winter temperature swings. Keep beds weed-free through spring and reduce watering as the lower leaves begin to brown ahead of harvest. Because it is a softneck type, the flexible stems can be braided for storage, and well-cured bulbs are prized in French markets for their long shelf life and delicate, slightly sweet garlic flavor.

planting.note: Separate cloves and plant pointed end up, about 2 inches deep, in fall; Solent Wight is an English hardneck bred on the Isle of Wight and requires a genuine cold winter to vernalize and divide into full-sized bulbs.

directions: Solent Wight is a British hardneck garlic developed on the Isle of Wight and grown for its large, purple-streaked bulbs and strong, well-rounded flavor suited to the cooler, damper UK climate. Plant cloves pointed end up in fall in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and mulch after the ground cools to guard against frost heaving. As with other hardnecks, cut off the curling scape in early summer to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size. Harvest once the lower leaves have browned, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy, shaded spot for a few weeks before trimming and storing.
